title: Cisco Systems goes public
what: Cisco Systems, a Menlo Park maker of routers that link different computer networks, sold 2.8 million shares to the public on February 16 at $18 each. The shares closed the first day at $22.25. The company, founded in 1984 by two Stanford computer staff, had sales of about $28 million in its last fiscal year and is profitable; the offering values it at roughly $224 million.
why: The listing beat (importance 1). The case for buying: a small, profitable, fast-growing company selling the boxes that connect the computer networks companies are building, years before the public internet. Whoever bought at the IPO held one of the best stocks of the decade.
source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/business-and-management/cisco-systems-goes-public (read 2026-10-03); market value at IPO from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cisco (read 2026-10-03)

title: Cisco breaks out as the market recovers
what: After a fall of about 22% between mid-July and October 11, the stock market started to recover in the second half of October. Cisco's shares were among the first to break out to new highs. The company has reported nine straight quarters of large earnings increases, its earnings have grown about 257% a year for three years, and analysts expect another 145% rise in 1991.
why: The start of Cisco's first great run: from the October 1990 low the shares more than tripled within twelve months (best twelve months +267%, 1990-08 to 1991-08). (Time check: title said 'the market turns', which assumes the October 1990 low held.)

title: Cisco's sales more than double again
what: Cisco closed its fiscal year at the end of July with sales of $183 million, up from $70 million the year before, and net income of $43 million. Demand for routers that tie together company networks of different makes keeps growing faster than the company can hire.
why: Fiscal 1991 confirms the growth story behind the 1990-91 run. The exact date of the annual report was not confirmed; the figures are the fiscal-year totals from the company histories.

title: Cisco doubles sales and signs up telephone companies
what: Cisco reported on November 9 that sales in the quarter to late October rose 99% to $126 million and net income 115% to $33 million. It announced partnerships with Alcatel, Olivetti, Bell Atlantic and US West and new router families, including an ISDN router for Japan.
why: Cisco starts to reach beyond corporate networks into the telephone carriers, the market that later made it the backbone supplier of the internet.

title: Cisco's profit doubles again
what: On May 6 Cisco reported sales of $172 million for the quarter to April 25, up 89% from a year earlier, and net income of $46 million, up 99%. For the first nine months of its fiscal year sales are up 94% to $444 million.
why: Another quarter of near-doubling; the shares jumped 31% in the month.

title: Cisco passes $1 billion in sales
what: Cisco reported on August 18 that sales for the fiscal year to July rose 92% to $1.24 billion and net income 83% to $315 million. Chief executive John Morgridge pointed to alliances with IBM, Microsoft and Alcatel and to the acquisitions of Crescendo and Newport Systems.
why: The shares recover from a spring slump (about -40% from January to July 1994) on proof that growth is intact.

title: Cisco buys StrataCom for about $4 billion
what: Cisco agreed on April 22 to acquire StrataCom, a maker of high-speed switches used by telephone carriers, in exchange for Cisco shares. Each StrataCom share is to be exchanged for one Cisco share or $50 of Cisco stock, putting the deal at around $4 billion, one of the largest in the industry. Chambers said Cisco will be the only vendor to offer connections across public and private networks.
why: Cisco buys its way into the carrier market as the internet takes off; acquisitions paid in its high-priced shares become its trademark.

title: Switch sales lift Cisco after a spring scare
what: Cisco's sales in the quarter to late April rose 52% to $1.65 billion from $1.09 billion a year earlier, driven by its Catalyst 5000 switches and its 2500, 4700 and 7500 router families. The shares had fallen by about a third in February and March.
why: The quarter ends a rare scare (-20% and -13% in February and March 1997, cause not confirmed in the sources read) and the shares rebound 31% in May. The figures are from the quarterly filing; the exact date of the earnings release in May was not confirmed.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000858877/000089161897002545/0000891618-97-002545.txt (10-Q for the quarter to April 27, 1997, read 2026-10-03)

title: Cisco pays $7.4 billion in stock to enter optical networking
what: Cisco agreed on August 25 to buy Cerent and Monterey Networks, two young makers of optical transport equipment, for a combined $7.4 billion in Cisco shares, its largest purchase so far. Earlier in the month it agreed to invest $1.05 billion in KPMG Consulting. Sales in the quarter to April had risen 44% to $3.15 billion.
why: The peak of the acquisition spree (17 companies in 1999). Cerent never earned back its price; by 2010 Cisco's optical revenue still did not justify it.

title: Cisco becomes the world's most valuable company
what: On March 27 Cisco's stock market value reached about $555 billion, more than Microsoft's, making it the most valuable company in the world. The shares were split two-for-one on March 22, the ninth split since the 1990 listing. Investors value Cisco as the company whose equipment carries the internet.
why: The peak (77.3 in game terms at the end of March 2000). From here the shares fell 86% to September 2002, and it took until December 2025 to regain the March 2000 closing high. (Time check: dropped 'briefly', which knows the lead was lost.)
source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/business-and-management/cisco-systems-goes-public (read 2026-10-03); split from https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/858877/0000891618-00-001722.txt (read 2026-10-03), count of splits from https://newsroom.cisco.com/c/r/newsroom/en/us/a/y1999/m05/cisco-systems-reports-third-quarter-earnings-and-two-for-one-stock-split.html (eighth split, read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cisco (read 2026-10-03)

title: Cisco says it sees no slowdown
what: Cisco's sales are still growing fast, and in November its chief strategy officer said: 'We haven't seen any sign of a slowdown.' Some component suppliers have begun to lower their forecasts. Cisco's shares are down by about 40% from their March high.
why: Hindsight: Cisco had locked into long supply commitments from May 2000 and its much-praised forecasting systems had no macroeconomic warning built in. Bookings were still up more than 70% in November and fell 30% below the year before within a few months (as Cisco reported in May 2001).

title: Cisco misses for the first time in years
what: Cisco reported on February 6 that sales in the quarter to January 27 rose 55% to $6.75 billion, but the result fell short of analysts' expectations, the company's first miss after years of beating forecasts. Chief executive John Chambers spoke of 'a brief pause in the current 10-year expansion of the U.S. economy' but said he remained confident about the next three to five years.
why: The first crack. The shares fell 37% in the month as investors realised the telecom and dot-com spending boom was ending.

title: Cisco announces the first layoffs in its history
what: On March 9 Cisco said it will cut 2,500 to 3,000 temporary and contract workers and 3,000 to 5,000 of its 44,000 regular employees, and take a charge of $300 million to $400 million. Chambers blamed 'the continuing slowdown in the U.S. economy and initial signs of a slowdown expanding to other parts of the world.' Only a year ago, on March 27, 2000, Cisco was worth $555 billion, more than any other company in the world.
why: For a company that had only ever hired, a shock to staff and shareholders alike. The shares fell another 33% in the month, to less than a quarter of their March 2000 value.

title: Cisco warns sales will fall and cuts 8,500 jobs
what: On April 16 Cisco said sales in the quarter to April will be about $4.7 billion, below the year before, after $6.7 billion in the previous quarter. It raised its job cuts to 8,500 and expects restructuring charges of $800 million to $1.2 billion. Chambers said the slowdown 'may be the fastest any industry our size has ever decelerated.'
why: The admission that the boom is over; the company now prepares for its first write-offs.

title: Cisco writes off $2.2 billion of inventory
what: Cisco reported on May 8 a net loss of $2.69 billion for the quarter to April, on sales of $4.73 billion, down 4% from a year earlier. The loss includes a $2.2 billion charge for excess inventory and $1.17 billion of restructuring costs. Chambers said bookings went from growth of more than 70% in November to a decline of 30% within a few months.
why: The defining write-off: parts ordered for growth that never came. It became the textbook case of a supply chain caught by a sudden stop.

title: Cisco ends a hard year with a loss
what: Cisco reported on August 7 a net loss of $1.01 billion for the fiscal year to July, against a profit of $2.67 billion the year before. Sales for the year still rose 18% to $22.3 billion, but fourth-quarter sales fell 25% to $4.3 billion. Chambers said the long-term outlook for the industry 'has not dramatically changed.'
why: The year in numbers. The shares fell 15% in August and another 25% in September after the attacks of September 11. (Time check: title called it Cisco's 'worst year', a judgement from hindsight.)

title: Cisco's sales grow again from the previous quarter
what: Cisco reported on November 5 sales of $4.4 billion for the quarter to October, 32% below a year earlier but 3% above the previous quarter, and a small profit before special charges. Chambers said the company gained market share while competitors' sales fell by high-teens percentages.
why: Signs that the fall has stopped; the shares had already rebounded strongly from their September lows. (Time check: title said 'from the bottom', which was known only later.)

title: Cisco grows again as tech stocks rebound
what: Cisco reported on November 6 that sales for the quarter to October rose 9% from a year earlier to $4.8 billion, with a profit of $618 million. It holds $21.2 billion in cash and investments. Chambers said Cisco is 'well positioned for an upturn, regardless of when it occurs.' Technology shares have rebounded since early October.
why: The bottom of the bear market: Cisco's low was September 2002 (10.5, -86% from the peak), and November brought a 33% rebound. (Time check: 'the market low' assumed the October 2002 low held.)

title: Cisco buys Linksys and enters the home
what: Cisco is buying Linksys, a maker of inexpensive routers for homes and small offices with about 300 employees and more than $500 million in annual sales. It is Cisco's first move into consumer products.
why: A turn towards consumers (later Scientific-Atlanta, Flip) that Cisco reversed a decade later when it sold Linksys in 2013. Wikipedia gives only the year 2003; the month of the announcement was not confirmed.

title: Cisco grows again, with sales of $22 billion
what: Cisco reported fiscal-year sales of $22.0 billion, up 16.8%, and net income of $4.4 billion. Sales in the quarter to July rose 26% from a year earlier to $5.9 billion.
why: Sales are nearly back to the fiscal 2001 level ($22.3 billion), but the share price stays at a quarter of its 2000 level: the market no longer pays for growth the way it did.

title: Cisco buys Scientific-Atlanta for $6.9 billion
what: Cisco agreed on November 18 to buy Scientific-Atlanta, a Georgia maker of cable television set-top boxes and network equipment, for $43 a share in cash, about $6.9 billion. Cisco's sales are now about $25 billion a year.
why: Cisco's biggest deal since Cerent, part of a push into the living room that it later abandoned (the set-top business was sold to Technicolor in 2015 for $600 million).

title: Cisco buys WebEx
what: Cisco has acquired WebEx, a company that runs online meetings and web conferences, for $3.2 billion. Cisco wants to sell collaboration software and video alongside its network equipment.
why: WebEx became a lasting Cisco business and came into its own when the pandemic sent office workers home in 2020.

title: Cisco grows 8% as the crisis deepens
what: Cisco reported sales of $10.3 billion for the quarter to October, up 8% from a year earlier, and net income of $2.2 billion. Chief executive John Chambers said the network matters more than ever in the current economic environment and that Cisco will prioritise its spending and invest in innovation.
why: Cisco stayed profitable through the financial crisis; the shares fell to about 15 by early 2009 and recovered within the year.

title: Cisco joins the Dow
what: Cisco was added to the Dow Jones Industrial Average on June 8. Its shares, which trade on the Nasdaq, now sit among the thirty best-known American blue chips.
why: Recognition as a blue chip at the bottom of the financial crisis; the shares had fallen to about 15 in early 2009.

title: Cisco bids $3 billion for Tandberg
what: Cisco agreed to make a cash offer of 153.5 Norwegian kroner a share, about $3.0 billion in all, for Tandberg, the Norwegian maker of video-conferencing systems. Tandberg's board recommends the offer.
why: One of the acquisitions that brought Cisco lasting technology (video conferencing), unlike several others of the period.

title: Cisco pays its first dividend
what: Cisco announced on March 18 its first cash dividend, 6 cents a share each quarter, payable April 20 to holders of record on March 31. At the current share price that is a yield of about 1.4%. The finance chief called it 'an important part of our commitment to bring value to shareholders.'
why: Cisco becomes an income stock. The dividend rose almost every year, to 42 cents a quarter by 2026, and from 2011 on the dividend was a large part of what Cisco shareholders earned.

title: Cisco cuts 6,500 jobs and closes Flip
what: On July 18 Cisco said it will cut about 6,500 jobs, around 9% of its regular workforce, as part of $1 billion of annual cost savings after disappointing profits. With the sale of a set-top box plant in Mexico and the closure of the Flip video camera business, about 12,000 jobs go in all. Competitors such as Juniper, HP and Huawei are pressing Cisco in its core markets.
why: The end of the consumer adventure and the start of the slow, cash-rich, dividend-paying Cisco.

title: Cisco to buy NDS for $5 billion
what: Cisco announced on March 15 that it will acquire NDS Group, a maker of software for pay-television operators, for $5 billion.
why: Another push into television video, which Cisco later sold off.

title: Cisco grows 6% and cuts 4,000 jobs
what: Cisco reported fiscal-year sales of $48.6 billion, up 6%, and said it will cut 4,000 jobs, about 6% of its workforce. In July it agreed to buy the security company Sourcefire for $2.7 billion.
why: A mature company growing in single digits and shifting towards security software.

title: Cisco's sales shrink and it cuts 8% of jobs
what: Cisco reported fiscal-year revenue of $47.1 billion, down 3%, and announced a restructuring that will eliminate about 8% of its global workforce, some 6,000 jobs, with charges of up to $700 million.
why: The low point of the hardware business before the shift to software and subscriptions under Robbins.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/858877/0001193125-14-308403.txt (8-K with press release, read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/858877/0001193125-14-308733.txt (8-K, read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cisco (read 2026-10-03)

title: Chuck Robbins to succeed John Chambers
what: Cisco named Chuck Robbins, its head of worldwide sales and a company veteran since 1997, as chief executive from July 26. John Chambers, chief executive since 1995, will remain chairman.
why: The end of the Chambers era; Robbins steered Cisco towards software, subscriptions and security.

title: Cisco buys AppDynamics on the eve of its IPO
what: Cisco agreed to buy AppDynamics, which monitors how business software performs, for $3.7 billion, a day before the start-up was to list its shares. Cisco is buying software companies to make up for slow growth in network hardware.
why: Part of the shift to software and recurring revenue under Robbins.

title: Cisco posts record quarterly revenue
what: Cisco reported record quarterly revenue of $12.8 billion, up 6%, and fiscal-year revenue of $49.3 billion, up 3%. Net income for the year was only $0.1 billion because of a $10.4 billion charge related to the new US tax law. It forecasts growth of 5% to 7% for the next quarter.
why: Recurring revenue (32% of the total) and buybacks lift the shares, +13% in August 2018.

title: Cisco warns of flat sales
what: Cisco reported fiscal-year sales of $51.7 billion, up 7%, but forecast growth of only 0% to 2% for the coming quarter. Chief executive Chuck Robbins pointed to the long-term opportunity.
why: A weak outlook, partly blamed on China, ends a two-year rally; the shares fell 16% in the month.

title: Covid-19 cuts Cisco's sales
what: Cisco reported fiscal-year revenue of $49.3 billion, down 5%, with fourth-quarter revenue down 9%, and forecast a decline of 9% to 11% for the next quarter. It has completed the acquisition of ThousandEyes, which monitors internet and cloud performance.
why: The pandemic year in numbers; the shares fell 10% in August 2020.

title: Lockdowns in China and the war hit Cisco
what: Cisco reported flat sales of $12.8 billion for the quarter to April and forecast a decline of 1% to 5.5% in the next quarter. Robbins said Covid lockdowns in China and the war in Ukraine hurt revenue; Cisco has stopped selling in Russia.
why: Supply-chain trouble in a falling market; Cisco lost about a third of its value in the first half of 2022.

title: Cisco to buy Splunk for $28 billion
what: Cisco agreed on September 21 to buy Splunk, a cybersecurity and data-monitoring software company, for $157 a share in cash, about $28 billion. It is by far the largest acquisition in Cisco's history.
why: Cisco bets on software and security for growth; the deal closed in March 2024.

title: Cisco cuts 5% of its staff as sales fall
what: Cisco reported on February 14 that sales fell 6% to $12.8 billion in the quarter to January, lowered its forecast for the year and announced a restructuring affecting about 5% of its workforce, more than 4,000 people. Telecom and cable customers have cut orders.
why: The low point of a post-pandemic hangover, just before AI data-centre demand lifted the company.

title: Cisco's share price passes its 2000 high
what: In December Cisco's shares closed above $80.06, the closing high of March 2000, for the first time in more than 25 years. Investors are buying it as a supplier of networking for AI data centres, including switches developed with Nvidia. Because Cisco has bought back many shares, its market value is still far below the 2000 peak.
why: A milestone for anyone who bought at the top in 2000: a quarter of a century to get even on price (dividends since 2011 aside).

title: AI orders send Cisco to a record
what: Cisco reported on May 13 record quarterly sales of $15.8 billion, up 12%, with product orders up 35%. It now expects $9 billion of orders for AI infrastructure this fiscal year, up from $5 billion, and raised its full-year forecast. It also announced a restructuring with up to $1 billion of charges to shift spending to silicon, optics, security and AI.
why: The biggest month for the shares (+32%) since 2001: Cisco is valued again as a growth company.
